ety.text: From Middle English moisture, from Old French moistour (“moisture, dampness, wetness”). Compare French moiteur.

senses.d: That which moistens or makes damp or wet; exuding fluid; liquid in small quantity.
ex:
I cannot weep; for all my body’s moisture
Scarce serves to quench my furnace-burning heart:
[…] all Exclusion of Open Aire, (which is euer Predatory) maintaineth the Body in his first Freshnesse, and Moisture:
[The organs of touch are excited] by the unceasing variations of the heat, moisture, and pressure of the atmosphere;

senses.d: Skin moisture noted as dry, moist, clammy, or diaphoretic as part of the skin signs assessment.

grp.label: the state of being moist — see also moistness

pt:humidade|PT.gl: European Portuguese standard spelling of umidade

ety.text: Proto-Indo-European *dʰeh₁-der. Proto-Italic *-iðos Latin -idus Latin ūmidus Latin hūmidus Proto-Indo-European *-teh₂ Proto-Indo-European *-ts Proto-Indo-European *-teh₂ts Proto-Italic *-tāts Latin -tās Latin hūmiditātembor. Portuguese humidade Borrowed from Latin hūmiditātem. By surface analysis, húmido + -idade.

The adjective is derived from Middle English moist, moiste [and other forms], from Anglo-Norman moist, moiste, moste, Middle French moiste, and Old French moiste, muste (“damp, moist, wet”) (modern French moite); further etymology uncertain, perhaps a blend of a Late Latin variant of Latin mūcidus (“mouldy, musty”) + a Late Latin derivative of Latin mustum (“unfermented or partially fermented grape juice or wine, must”). The noun is derived from the adjective.

chain.g: to make moist or wet; to become moist or wet

ety.text: From Middle English moisten, moist, moiste (“to make moist or wet; to soak in liquid; to become moist or wet; to provide with moisture or water; to satisfy thirst with liquor or water, slake”) [and other forms], and then either: * from Anglo-Norman muster (“to make moist or wet”), Middle French moistir, and Old French moistir (“to make moist or wet; to become moist or wet”) (compare enmoistir; modern French moitir), from Old French moiste, muste (“damp, moist, wet”) (see etymology 1) + -ir (suffix forming infinitives of second conjugation verbs); or * from Middle English moist, moiste (adjecti…

senses.d: Characterized by the presence of moisture; not dry; slightly wet; damp.
ex: Will theſe moyſt Trees, / That haue out-liu'd the Eagle, page thy heeles / And skip when thou point'ſt out?
[Y]et the North-ſide [of the pyramids of Giza] moſt worne, by reaſon of the humiditie of the Northerne wind, which here is the moiſteſt.

senses.d: Of eyes: wet with tears; tearful; also (obsolete), watery due to some illness or to old age.
ex: And on the banner which stood near / He glanced a look of holy pride, / And his moist eyes were glorified; […]
Eyes moist, he [Maurice Stans] hugged one of his attorneys and later said: "I feel like I've been reborn."

senses.d: Of a climate, the weather, etc.: damp, humid, rainy.
ex: The time is early in the evening; the weather moist and raw.

senses.d: Of the vagina: sexually lubricated due to sexual arousal; of a woman: sexually aroused, turned on.
ex: He slid a finger in me, checking to make sure I was moist and ready for him.

senses.d: Characterized by the presence of some fluid such as mucus, pus, etc.
Of sounds of internal organs (especially as heard through a stethoscope): characterized by the sound of air bubbling through a fluid.
Pertaining to one of the four essential qualities formerly believed to be present in all things, characterized by wetness; also, having a significant amount of this quality.
ex: [T]he moiſt ſtarre, / Vpon whoſe influence Neptunes Empier ſtands, / Was ſicke almoſt to doomeſday with eclipſe, […]
O pardon me, my liege, but for my teares, / The moiſt impediments vnto my ſpeech, / I had foreſtald this deere and deep rebuke, […]
And the moiſt daughters of huge Atlas ſtroue / Into the Ocean deepe to driue their weary droue.
Ere twice in murke and occidentall dampe / Moiſt Heſperus hath quench'd her ſleepy Lampe: […]

senses.d: To make (something) moist or wet; to moisten.
ex: He calleth for a ſponge (ſaith Theodoritus) and therevvith moiſteth and vvaſsheth Simeones mouthe, and then geueth him the holy Sacrament.
Now no more / The iuyce of Egypts Grape ſhall moyſt this lip.

senses.d: To inspire, to refresh (someone); also, to soften (one's heart).
To have an effect of moistening or wetting.
ex: Auyſing the bright bemes of theſe fayer Iyes / where he is that myn oft moiſteth & waſſheth
Againe, nothyng moiſteth ſoner then water. Therefore, a wepyng eye cauſeth muche moiſture, and prouoketh teares.

grp.label: characterized by the presence of moisture; slightly wet

Inherited from Old French moiste, muste, from a cross between Vulgar Latin *mucidus (from Latin mūcidus) with forms of mustum; cf. *mustidus.
Inherited from Latin hūmidus or ūmidus.

pt:úmido.gl: humid; damp; moist (somewhat wet or watery)
